skill.name: Persuasive tricks: exaggeration, "everyone's doing it", rhetorical questions
skill.why: Persuaders use tricks to push you. Spot the trick and it loses its power.
skill.how: Ask: is it blown up, 'join the crowd', or a question with the answer built in?

steps.say: My pies are so hot they could melt a ute! Could that really happen?

show.text: My pies are so hot they could melt a ute!

options.text: asking you a question
options.reason: There's no question here. Is a pie really that hot?

options.text: making it sound way bigger than it is
telling you a fact you could check
options.reason: Could a pie melt a metal ute? Mo knows it can't. He's blowing it up.

steps.win: Yes! I blew it way up to sound amazing. That's exaggeration. Its fancy name is hyperbole.

steps.say: Next trick. Here's my sign for Pie Club.

show.text: Your mates have already joined. Don't get left behind!

steps.ask: What does the sign want you to do?

options.text: count how many mates joined
options.reason: The sign doesn't want you to count. It wants you to follow.

options.text: answer a question
options.reason: There's no question here. Who does it say has joined?

options.text: join the crowd, so you don't miss out

steps.win: Yes! Join the crowd or miss out. That trick is 'everyone's doing it'. Some call it the bandwagon trick.

steps.say: Last trick. Here's a question on my sign.

show.text: Who wouldn't want a free pie?

steps.ask: Does Mo want you to answer it?

options.text: No. The answer is built in.
Yes. He wants a list of names.
options.reason: Would Mo wait for names? What answer does he hope you will think?

options.text: Yes. It's a quiz.
options.reason: In a quiz you work out the answer. Mo already knows the one he wants.

steps.win: Right! You're meant to think, 'Everyone would!' That's a rhetorical question: the answer is built in.

steps.say: Careful! Not every question is a trick. Some need a real answer.

show.text: Who wouldn't want a free pie?
show.nudge: Mo already knows the answer he wants: everyone would! Try another.

show.text: What size pie would you like?
Why eat soggy sandwiches when pies exist?
show.nudge: The answer's built in: don't eat soggy sandwiches! Try another.

steps.ask: Tap the real question, the one Mo needs you to answer.
steps.win: Yes! Mo really needs to know your size. A real question is no trick.

steps.say: Careful! A crowd or a big claim can be a plain fact too.

show.text: Two hundred kids came last year.
show.nudge: That's a count from last year. Does it push you to join?

show.text: Your whole class has tickets. Don't miss out!
The ferry is so popular it sells out on Fridays.
show.nudge: That could really happen. Is it blown up, or just true?

steps.ask: Tap the line that uses a trick.
steps.win: Yes! It pushes you to join the crowd. The other two are just information.

steps.say: Spot the trick. Then ask: is it actually true?

show.text: Three million players have joined Lava League!

steps.ask: Does that prove the game is good for you?

options.text: Yes. That many people can't be wrong.
options.reason: Lots of people can like something you would hate. Does the crowd know you?

options.text: Yes, because the number is real.
options.reason: Even if the number is true, it's about them, not you.

options.text: No. Lots of players doesn't mean it suits you.

steps.win: Yes! Answering back like that is called a rebuttal. Now the trick has lost its power.

encounters.frame: Year 6 student Priya is campaigning for a longer lunch break at Bluster Rock School. She gave this speech at assembly.
encounters.text: Good morning, everyone. My name is Priya, and I am here to ask the school council to make our lunch break longer. At the moment, we have twenty-five minutes to eat our lunch, go to the toilet, fill our drink bottles and play. By the time most of us reach the oval, the bell is already ringing. Last Tuesday, I timed the canteen queue. It took me nine minutes just to buy a sausage roll. Dr Kim Nguyen, a researcher who studies children's health, says that kids who play outside at lunch concentrate better in the afternoon. I have spoken to the canteen staff, and they say that a longer lunch would also mean shorter queues. The school day would finish fifteen minutes later, but most parents I asked said they would not mind. So I have one question for the council. Is twenty-five minutes really enough time to eat, play and get ready to learn again? Please vote yes at the council meeting on Thursday. Thank you for listening, and please put your apple cores in the bin, not on the oval.
encounters.prompt: Priya could have said, 'Twenty-five minutes is not enough.' Why did she ask it as a question instead?
encounters.success: A rhetorical question lets listeners answer it themselves. Agreeing in your own head feels like your idea, not Priya's.

options.text: She wants the council to tell her how many minutes would be enough.
options.reason: Nobody is asked for a number. The answer, 'no', is already built in.

options.text: She isn't sure, so she's asking the council for advice.
options.reason: Priya gives a whole speech of reasons. She is sure of her answer.

options.text: Listeners think 'no' for themselves, so it feels like their own idea.
A question blows the problem up, so it sounds far worse than it is.
options.reason: Blowing up is exaggeration. Nothing in that question is bigger than it really is.

encounters.frame: A ferry company has mailed a glossy brochure to every house on Bluster Rock. Tully is reading it with a pencil.
encounters.text: INTRODUCING THE BLUSTER EXPRESS. From the first of March, our brand-new passenger ferry will run between Bluster Rock and the mainland six times a day, seven days a week. The ferry seats 120 passengers on two decks, with a cafe on the lower deck and an open-air viewing platform at the top, where dolphins are often spotted in the channel. The crossing takes forty minutes, and bicycles travel free of charge. The ferry carries people and bicycles only. Cars and trailers must still take the coast road, which is a three-hour drive around the bay. Adult tickets are $18 each way, and children under twelve travel for half price. Why would anyone endure three hours behind the wheel when they could be sipping a hot chocolate on the water? Tickets can be bought online or at the kiosk on the jetty. The cafe sells hot chocolate, toasted sandwiches and lamingtons. On very rough days the ferry may not run, and ticket holders will get a text message. Tully underlined the hot chocolate question and wrote 'Is that actually true?' beside it.
encounters.prompt: The hot chocolate question has its answer built in: nobody would drive. Which line shows that some people still have to?
encounters.success: Anyone with a car or trailer still has to drive. Asking 'Is it actually true?' takes the trick's power away.

options.text: Bicycles travel free of charge.
options.reason: That's a reason to take the ferry. It gives nobody a reason to drive.

options.text: The coast road is a three-hour drive around the bay.
options.reason: This says how long the drive takes. It doesn't show that anyone has to make it.

options.text: Cars and trailers must still take the coast road.
Children under twelve travel for half price.
options.reason: Cheaper tickets push people onto the ferry, not into a car.

encounters.frame: The new Red Rock Wildlife Park has printed a brochure. Wren read it with a pencil in her hand, marking every trick.
encounters.text: WELCOME TO THE RED ROCK WILDLIFE PARK. Nestled at the foot of Bluster Rock, our park is home to more than forty kinds of native animals, from tiny dunnarts to towering emus. Our keepers care for injured and orphaned animals and, where possible, return them to the wild. You'll meet every animal in Australia in one afternoon. The park is big enough to need its own little train, which stops at the aviary, the waterhole and the koala walk. Last year, 60,000 people visited the park. Every family on your street has been. Yours is the only one left. Who could resist meeting a bilby up close? Keeper talks are held every hour on the hour, and visitors can help feed the kangaroos at 2 pm. Entry costs $22 for adults and $11 for children. Is your child under four? Then entry is free. The park cafe sells sandwiches, ice creams and hot drinks, and picnic tables sit under the coolabah trees beside the waterhole. Wheelchairs and prams can travel on every path, and a night tour runs on Friday evenings in summer.
encounters.prompt: Match each line from the brochure to its trick, or to 'no trick'.
encounters.success: Every animal is blown up and your street is the crowd. The real question and true facts are no trick.

items.text: You'll meet every animal in Australia in one afternoon.
items.reason: The park has about forty kinds of animal. That's nowhere near every animal in Australia.

items.text: Every family on your street has been. Yours is the only one left.
items.reason: This says everyone near you has been, so your family had better join them.

items.text: Who could resist meeting a bilby up close?
items.reason: The brochure isn't asking. It builds in the answer: nobody could.

items.text: Is your child under four? Then entry is free.
items.reason: This question needs a real answer. Your answer tells you what you'll pay.

items.text: The park is big enough to need its own little train.
items.reason: A big claim, but true. The train really runs, so nothing is blown up.

items.text: Last year, 60,000 people visited the park.
items.reason: That's a crowd, but nobody is pushed to join it. It's plain information.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote notes on a ghost tour brochure for the crew. Indi checked them and found one mistake.
encounters.text: THE MIDNIGHT HOMESTEAD TOUR. Step back in time at the old Crowley homestead, built of sandstone in 1884 and empty since 1914. The island's first car did not arrive until 1911, so the Crowleys travelled by horse and cart. Guided by lantern light, you will explore the cellar, the shearers' quarters and the bedroom where, according to local legend, a rocking chair still rocks on windless nights. Line 1: 'Why settle for another dull evening in front of the television?' Line 2: 'The homestead is so old that it was built before the first car came to the island.' Line 3: 'Our guides tell stories so chilling that visitors' hair has turned white on the spot.' Tours leave from the homestead gate at 9 pm every Friday and Saturday, and last about ninety minutes. The track is uneven, so sturdy shoes and a torch are recommended. Tickets are $25, or $15 for children over ten. Hot chocolate is served in the kitchen at the end of every tour, beside the old iron stove that Elsie Crowley once cooked on.

encounters.frame: Mo has started an online campaign to raise money for a floating restaurant. The crew is worried. So is the Squawkle.
encounters.text: MO'S FLOATING FEAST: HELP ME BUILD IT! Hello, friends of Bluster Rock. For years, I have dreamed of opening a restaurant on a raft in the middle of Bluster Bay, where diners can enjoy my cooking while watching the sunset over the rock. I have found a second-hand pontoon that can hold eight tables, and a local builder has agreed to fit a kitchen and a roof. The whole project will cost $14,000. If you give $20, you will get a free bowl of my famous seaweed spag bol. If you give $100, I will name a dish after you. Since the campaign began, more than four hundred islanders have pledged their support, so don't be the last to join. The menu will include fish-finger custard, gum-leaf pancakes and sardine trifle, all cooked fresh on board. The harbour master has asked me to add life jackets for every diner, which I think is a bit much. Gus has offered to design a slime-powered motor, and Tully has worked out that there is a 64 per cent chance the raft will float.
encounters.prompt: Tully wants to answer back to the line about four hundred islanders. Which reply takes away the trick's power?
encounters.success: Ask: is it actually true? Pledges are about the crowd, not the raft. Tully says it might not float.

options.text: Four hundred is too small to count as a real crowd.
options.reason: Size isn't the problem. Even a huge crowd wouldn't prove the raft floats.

options.text: A crowd of pledges doesn't prove the raft will float.
Mo probably made that number up, so just ignore it.
options.reason: The number might be true. Ask whether the crowd proves anything.

options.text: Then I'd better give $20 too, before it's too late.

encounters.frame: Maxx is auctioning a painting on his stream to raise money for his 'Rescue Fund'. Indi is watching, with her moustache pen ready.
encounters.text: 'Hey, Vantafam! Tonight, I'm auctioning something truly special to raise money for my Rescue Fund. This is a painting of me, by me, called Gold Is Forever. I painted it on the deck of the Vantadome using real gold-coloured paint, and it's signed in the bottom corner. It measures one metre by two metres, and the frame is solid wood. Bidding starts at $500, and the winner will receive a certificate signed by me. The auction closes at midnight. Over twenty thousand of you are already bidding, so bid now before it's too late. Don't those poor Creatures deserve a hero like me? Every cent goes to the Rescue Fund. Stay gold!' Indi copied the bidding line into her notebook. Then she crossed out the second half, so it said only: 'Over twenty thousand of you are already bidding.' Wren muttered that she'd love to know where the money really goes. Indi's moustache pen hovered over the screen, but she decided to take notes instead. Gus asked whether gold-coloured paint is the same as gold. It is not. Mo asked whether the painting came with a pie.

encounters.success: On its own, the number is information. 'Bid now before it's too late' turns it into everyone's doing it.
